title: Senior At-Home Care
desc: Plan and deliver safe, respectful at-home support for older adults: daily living, safety, medicines reminders, dignity and when to call for help.
outcomes: Explain the needs, rights and dignity of an older person at home.
Find fall, fire and medicine risks in a home.
Judge when a situation needs a professional or emergency help.
Build a written care routine and a family communication plan.
task: Produce a person-centred home care plan for a practice case, with a home safety check, daily routine, emergency card and carer wellbeing plan.
condition: A practice case or a consenting family, a phone, forms, two peers and a qualified nurse or care mentor. Nursing procedures are outside scope.
standard: Plan respects the person's wishes; safety check finds and fixes at least 8 risks; emergency card is complete; no clinical task is done outside training; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Family carers, home-care assistants, community volunteers, care entrepreneurs.
evidence: care plan, home safety checklist, routine, emergency card, carer plan
modules: Respect and dignity
Understand
Care starts with the person, not the task.
Ask what they want; offer choices; use their name.
Protect privacy in washing, dressing and toilet care.
Never treat an adult like a child.
Mr Rao prefers tea at 7; the carer plans around it and keeps the bathroom door closed.
Write a "what matters to me" page with the person.
Page uses their words.
Home safety check
Analyse
Most harm at home is preventable.
Falls: loose rugs, poor light, wet floors, no rails.
Fire and electrical hazards; gas safety.
Easy-to-reach items and clear paths.
A carer removes a loose mat and fits a night light, ending night-time stumbles.
Complete a checklist for one home.
At least 8 risks found, each with a fix and date.
Daily living support
Apply
Support independence, not dependence.
Meals, drinks and nutrition; assist with mobility; hygiene.
Do with, not for, whenever possible.
Safe lifting: ask for training; use aids.
The carer sets out clothes in order and lets Mrs Iyer dress herself.
Plan a day routine with times.
Routine covers meals, fluids, movement, rest and social time.
Medicines and health reminders
Apply
Carers remind; clinicians decide.
Use a pill organiser prepared by a pharmacist or nurse.
Record what was taken; never change doses.
Report new symptoms promptly.
A weekly box with morning and evening slots reduces missed doses.
Create a reminder chart and record sheet.
Chart matches the prescriber's list.
Mind, mood and memory
Apply
Loneliness and forgetfulness are common.
Keep routine; use calendars and clocks; encourage activity.
Be patient; do not argue about facts when kind redirection works.
Watch for sudden confusion, which can mean illness.
A daily 15-minute walk and a call to a grandchild lifts mood.
Plan a weekly social schedule.
Includes five activities.
Emergencies and when to call
Evaluate
Know the line between watch and act.
Call emergency services for chest pain, stroke signs, serious fall, breathing trouble.
Call the doctor for fever, new pain, poor eating.
Keep an emergency card at the door.
Face drooping and slurred speech: call emergency now, note the time.
Make an emergency card.
Includes numbers, allergies, medicines, contacts.
Family and carer wellbeing
Evaluate
Carers burn out.
Share the load; take breaks; ask for respite.
Keep a shared log or group message.
Seek local support groups.
Siblings take alternate weekends; stress drops.
Write a carer plan.
Plan names who, when, what.
Review and improve
Create
Care plans change as needs change.
Review monthly or after any event.
Track weight, sleep, mood, falls.
Celebrate good days.
After a fall, a rail and a physiotherapy visit are added.
Present your plan review.
Changes are dated and agreed with the person.
quiz: Loose rugs, poor light, wet floors.
Chest pain, stroke signs, serious fall, breathing trouble.
Support independence by helping only as needed.
What is sudden confusion a sign of?
What goes on an emergency card?
rubric: Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
Checked, dated and explained to others
local: Care rules, licences and background checks differ by place.
ladder: L1: learner can name basic needs of an older person.
L2: learner knows dignity and safety rules.
L3: learner can complete a home safety check.
L4: learner can deliver a daily routine.
L5: learner can handle medicines reminders and emergencies.
L6: learner can coordinate a team.
L7: learner can audit a care plan.
